raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old man with HIV and a history of cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma presented with left eyelid droop and left-sided facial numbness five days after restarting antiretroviral therapy following a long hiatus. He was diagnosed with HIV 21 years prior and had a nadir CD4 cell count of 107. His CD4 cell count when he restarted his antiretroviral regimen was 159 cells/mm3, viral load 511,000 c/mL. He had been intermittently compliant with antiretroviral therapy in the past and since resumption of therapy. In 2005, he had a recurrence of Kaposi's sarcoma and received five cycles of paclitaxel with clinical remission by 2006. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable at the time and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was read as having no significant abnormalities. His symptoms initially were stable, but in the subsequent two months, they worsened, with hypoesthesia and paresthesia over all three branches of the trigeminal nerve on the left, severe headaches, ataxia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. He also began to experience fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. A repeat MRI revealed enhancing leptomeningeal masses with associated mass effect involving the trigeminal nerve, middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, and upper spinal cord. Review of his prior MRI showed a suggestion of enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve intradurally. 
A lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein (205 g/dL), slightly depressed glucose (45 g/dL), with 106 leukocytes (32% lymphocytes, 26% monocytes, and 42% unclassified cells), and no erythrocytes. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) cytology was notable for atypical appearing cells, which were suspicious for, but not sufficient for a primary diagnosis of malignancy (see Figure 2(a)). CSF flow cytometry demonstrated no clonal B- or T-cell populations, and IGH gene rearrangement was not detected by PCR. CSF PCR for EBV was negative.
A bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable and core needle biopsy of a modestly enlarged retroperitoneal lymph node showed no evidence of lymphoproliferative disease. There was no evidence of pleural, peritoneal, or pericardial effusions on computed tomography and ultrasound studies. A positron emission tomography with computed tomography (PET/CT) was then performed and demonstrated increased uptake at the known cerebellopontine lesion, as well as in the posterior inferior wall and papillary muscle of the left ventricle of the heart (Figure 1). An endomyocardial biopsy of the left ventricle was performed via left heart catheterization. Pathology revealed large atypical discohesive cells infiltrating the myocardium. Immunostains of the atypical lymphoid cells were strongly KSHV+ (Figure 2), MUM1/IRF4+, CD79a rare+, CD20-. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) using a probe for EBER showed no staining. Comparison with the CSF specimens showed that these atypical cells were morphologically similar to the suspicious cells in the CSF (Figure 2(a)).
A preliminary diagnosis of large B-cell lymphoma was made based on morphologic appearance, and the patient was initiated on treatment with R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) along with intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, and hydrocortisone for the leptomeningeal disease. He was observed on telemetry for one week without cardiac ectopy and was discharged home. One day following discharge, he had syncope and was found to be in ventricular tachycardia with preserved blood pressure, for which he was treated with lidocaine and amiodarone with successful conversion to sinus rhythm. CD20 staining on his pathology returned negative and so treatment with cycle 2 was changed to EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin) without rituximab. High-dose systemic methotrexate was included to treat the CNS disease. Six weeks into treatment, restaging PET CT imaging showed no persistent FDG-avid disease of the heart, and MRI showing significant resolution of his intracranial tumor. Spinal fluid examination demonstrated no persistent circulating disease in the CSF. Clinically, his headaches, dysarthria, and dysphagia improved, but he still had numbness of his left face along the V1 and V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve along with an upper motor facial nerve palsy on the left. Some residual gait ataxia was notable on examination.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presenting with left eyelid ptosis and left facial numbness five days after restarting combination antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient resumed combination antiretroviral therapy after a prolonged hiatus; five days later, he noted left eyelid droop and ipsilateral facial numbness. Over the subsequent two months, symptoms progressed with severe headaches, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and hypoesthesia/paresthesia across all three divisions of the left trigeminal nerve, prompting extensive neuro-oncologic investigation.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 21 years prior with intermittent compliance (nadir CD4 107 cells/mcL; resumption CD4 159 cells/mm3, viral load 511,000 copies/mL). History of cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma in 2005, treated with five cycles of paclitaxel with complete clinical remission by 2006.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left-sided facial numbness, ptosis, headaches, dysarthria, dysphagia, gait ataxia, fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss; negative for focal limb weakness or bowel/bladder incontinence. Home medications: combination antiretroviral therapy. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Neurologic examination: left eyelid ptosis, sensory deficit (hypoesthesia and paresthesia) across V1, V2, and V3 branches of the left trigeminal nerve, left upper motor facial nerve paresis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and gait ataxia. Remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis: leukocytes 106/mcL (32% lymphocytes, 26% monocytes, 42% unclassified atypical cells), protein elevated at 205 g/dL (as documented in text), glucose depressed at 45 g/dL, erythrocytes: 0. CSF PCR for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): negative. CSF flow cytometry: no clonal B- or T-cell population; IGH gene rearrangement by PCR: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: enhancing leptomeningeal masses with mass effect involving the left trigeminal nerve, middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, and upper spinal cord (retrospective review showed subtle enhancement of left trigeminal nerve intradurally). Bone marrow biopsy: unremarkable. Retroperitoneal lymph node core biopsy: no lymphoproliferative disease. Chest/abdominal/pelvic CT and ultrasound: no pleural, peritoneal, or pericardial effusions. 18F-FDG PET/CT: increased uptake at the left cerebellopontine angle lesion and hypermetabolic foci in the posterior inferior wall and papillary muscle of the left cardiac ventricle. Left ventricular endomyocardial biopsy: large atypical discohesive lymphoid cells infiltrating the myocardium, strongly positive for KSHV/HHV-8, MUM1/IRF4, and rare CD79a, negative for CD20 and EBER in situ hybridization.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Extracavitary solid-variant Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV/HHV-8)-associated large B-cell lymphoma / primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) with myocardial infiltration and leptomeningeal involvement in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Confirmed by endomyocardial biopsy showing atypical discohesive large lymphoid cells strongly positive for KSHV and MUM1/IRF4 (CD20-negative, EBER-negative), morphologically matching atypical cells in CSF cytology. EBV-driven lymphoma ruled out by negative EBER and negative CSF EBV PCR. Management & Outcome: Initially treated empirically with R-CHOP plus intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, and hydrocortisone; after CD20 returned negative, switched to EPOCH without rituximab, augmented with high-dose intravenous methotrexate for CNS penetration. Post-discharge ventricular tachycardia was successfully converted with lidocaine and amiodarone. At 6 weeks, restaging PET/CT demonstrated complete cardiac metabolic response, brain MRI showed marked intracranial tumor regression, and CSF cytology cleared, with substantial clinical improvement in headaches, dysarthria, and dysphagia.
